content.title: About
content.content: Ham or pork with stuffing is a boiled or smoked pork product that is filled with various fillings (such as breadcrumbs, spices, vegetables, or mushrooms). It is commonly used in festive dishes, appetizers, and sandwiches. The product offers a juicy flavor, aromatic spices, and a pleasant texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Stuffing meat dates back to ancient times and was popular in European cuisine.
Ham with stuffing is often prepared as large loaves that are later sliced thinly.
Different regions use unique mixtures: Poland – sauerkraut, Italy – cheese and herbs, Russia – buckwheat and onion.
Smoking gives the product its characteristic aroma and extends shelf life.
Ham with stuffing is frequently served cold as an appetizer, but it can also be reheated in the oven.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Pork provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Ham contains thiamine, riboflavin, niacin, and vitamin B12, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The product supplies iron, zinc, and phosphorus, important for blood formation and bones.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and fat helps maintain a feeling of fullness longer.

items.title: Benefits of spices
items.content: Fillings often include garlic, paprika, or herbs, which have antioxidant properties.

items.title: High salt content
items.content: Ham is often salty; excessive salt intake can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Pork contains saturated fats that may affect cholesterol levels when consumed frequently.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some hams may contain nitrites and other preservatives, which raise concerns for certain consumers.

items.title: Allergy to spices
items.content: Fillings can include nuts, seafood, or other allergens.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Ham with stuffing can be eaten cold as sliced meat, added to salads, sandwiches, and appetizer platters. It can also be gently warmed in the oven or on a skillet to enhance the spice aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store ham in its original packaging or an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0 °C to +4 °C. It keeps up to 7 days after opening. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C, where it retains quality for up to 3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Asian mushrooms are dried edible fungi from the Pleurotaceae family, widely used in Asian cuisine. After rehydrating in water they regain their texture and can be cooked like fresh mushrooms, offering a delicate umami aroma and a mildly sweet flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dried Asian mushrooms are a staple in soups, stews, and stir‑fries.
When properly soaked they expand 5–7 times their original volume.
They are rich in beta‑glucans, which support immune function.
Traditionally used in Chinese medicine to aid digestion.
They store well for long periods without losing flavor.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Mushrooms provide plant‑based protein that helps maintain muscle mass.

items.title: Low calorie density
items.content: They are suitable for weight‑controlled diets due to their modest calorie content.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: B2, B3 and B5 vitamins support energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains essential minerals
items.content: Potassium, selenium and copper contribute to heart and nervous system health.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Beta‑glucans stimulate activity of immune cells.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to mushrooms.

items.title: Mycotoxin contamination
items.content: Improperly dried mushrooms can contain toxins; purchase from reputable sources.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large portions may cause gas and bloating.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Soak dried mushrooms in warm water for 20–30 minutes, drain, and use in soups, sauces, stir‑fries or stews. Add them to rice, noodles, or vegetable mixes. For extra aroma, briefly sauté after rehydration.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep dried mushrooms in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Properly stored they retain quality for 2–3 years. Once rehydrated, use within 1–2 days and store in the refrigerator.

content.title: About
content.content: Peanuts, honey roasted are roasted peanuts coated with a sweet honey glaze. The peanut (Arachis hypogaea) is a legume, not a true nut, cultivated in warm climates worldwide. The honey‑roasted version combines a crunchy texture, nutty flavor and a subtle sweetness.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peanuts develop underground: after pollination the flower stalk bends down and the pod matures beneath the soil.
Honey‑roasted peanuts are popular in both Asian and American snack culture and are used in desserts and trail mixes.
Peanuts are a good source of resistant starch, which supports a healthy gut microbiome.
Honey in the glaze adds natural antimicrobial properties, extending shelf life.
In the United States honey‑roasted peanuts rank among the top‑10 best‑selling snack products.

items.title: Plant‑based protein source
items.content: Peanuts contain about 25 % protein, providing essential amino acids for vegetarians and vegans.

items.title: Monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats
items.content: The fat profile helps maintain healthy cholesterol levels and supports heart health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Rich in niacin, thiamine and folate, peanuts aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: They provide magnesium, phosphorus, iron and zinc, important for bones, blood and immune function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Polyphenols and resveratrol in peanuts help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Nut and legume allergy
items.content: Peanuts are one of the most common allergens and can trigger severe reactions.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Because of their fat content, peanuts are energy‑dense; portion control is advisable.

items.title: Added sugar in the glaze
items.content: Honey‑roasted varieties contain extra sugar, which may be unsuitable for diabetics or low‑sugar diets.

items.title: Aflatoxin risk
items.content: Improper storage can lead to mold growth producing aflatoxins; purchase from reputable sources.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Honey‑roasted peanuts are perfect as a snack, tossed into granola, yogurt, baked goods, or used in Asian dishes such as salads and noodle stir‑fries.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct light. For longer storage, refrigerate or freeze to prevent fat oxidation.

content.title: About
content.content: A pumpernickel roll is a small, round bun made from whole‑grain rye flour. It has a dense, slightly tangy crust and a soft, aromatic crumb. Pumpernickel rolls are often used as a base for sandwiches, appetizers, or as a side for soups and salads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pumpernickel bread is a traditional staple in Scandinavian and Eastern European cuisines.
Its dark color comes from the use of malt and caramel, not artificial coloring.
Rye flour provides more fiber and minerals than wheat flour, making the roll more nutritious.
In some regions the rolls are baked with caraway or coriander seeds for extra flavor.
Pumpernickel rolls are a common component of the classic Swedish open‑face sandwich (smörgås).

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Rye flour contains both soluble and insoluble fiber, which supports digestive health.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Compared with white bread, pumpernickel rolls raise blood sugar more slowly, beneficial for glucose control.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The roll provides thiamine, niacin, and folate, essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: It supplies magnesium, iron, and zinc, supporting muscle function and immunity.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: Complex carbs and fiber help you feel full longer.

items.title: Grain allergy
items.content: People allergic to wheat or other grains may react to pumpernickel rolls.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some recipes add salt, so those monitoring sodium should check the label.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Pumpernickel rolls contain gluten and are not suitable for individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pumpernickel rolls are perfect for sandwiches with fish, ham, or vegetables, sliced in half and spread with butter or cream cheese. They also make a hearty side for soups, stews, or as a base for open‑face appetizers.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep rolls in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, refrigerate (up to a week) or freeze (up to 3 months). Discard any rolls that show mold or a stale, sour smell.

content.title: About
content.content: Canned chicken soup 1906 is a ready‑to‑eat soup made from chicken meat, vegetables and spices, sealed in an airtight can. The sterilisation process preserves flavor and nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: First released in 1906 as a travel and expedition ration.
Aluminium can provides a long shelf life without added preservatives.
The chicken broth base contains collagen, giving the soup a rich taste.
1906 soup was widely used in military rations during World War I.
The original recipe used only natural spices, no artificial flavourings.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Chicken meat supplies high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamin B6 and niacin, supporting metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Provides iron, phosphorus and potassium, important for blood formation and electrolyte balance.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: Warm broth aids digestion, especially during colds.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The soup is mostly water, helping maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Canned soup often contains a lot of salt, which can be an issue for hypertension.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some individuals may have an allergic reaction to chicken or added spices.

items.title: Bisphenol A in packaging
items.content: Aluminium cans may have trace BPA; choose BPA‑free labelled products when possible.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: While the original formula lacked them, modern versions may include stabilisers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the soup in a pot or microwave until boiling, stirring occasionally. You can add fresh vegetables, herbs or noodles for variety. Serve hot, optionally seasoned with black pepper.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened can in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 2‑3 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Spaghetti and meatballs dinner is a ready‑to‑heat frozen meal produced by NFS. The package contains spaghetti, a seasoned tomato sauce, and meatballs made from beef and pork. It is designed for quick preparation in a microwave or on the stovetop in 5‑7 minutes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish is based on the classic Italian-American spaghetti‑and‑meatballs recipe popular since the mid‑20th century.
Meatballs are a 70/30 blend of beef to pork, providing juiciness and a rich flavor.
The tomato sauce is made from ripe tomatoes, onion, garlic and basil, without artificial coloring.
The frozen product has been tested to retain pasta texture after microwave reheating.
Packaging is made from recyclable plastic, meeting NFS’s sustainability standards.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: The meatballs deliver about 12 g of protein per serving, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Beef provides heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Tomato sauce – source of lycopene
items.content: Lycopene is an antioxidant that supports heart health.

items.title: Carbohydrates for energy
items.content: Spaghetti supplies complex carbs that provide sustained energy and satiety.

items.title: Low added sugar
items.content: The meal contains no added sugars, making it suitable for moderate sugar intake.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Spaghetti is made from wheat, so the product is not suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: The sauce may contain trace dairy ingredients; check the label if you have a dairy allergy.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: The tomato sauce provides about 500 mg of sodium per serving; individuals monitoring salt intake should account for this.

items.title: Requires thorough heating
items.content: Insufficient heating can leave the product unsafe; follow the recommended time and temperature.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the package in the microwave (or on the stovetop) according to the instructions, stir, and serve hot. Optional toppings include grated Parmesan, fresh basil, or vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen meal at –18 °C or lower. Once the package is opened, consume within 24 hours and store in the refrigerator.

content.title: About
content.content: Steak is a cut of beef, typically taken from the rib, sirloin, or tenderloin. It has a rich, meaty flavor, firm texture, and a distinctive aroma that intensifies when seared over high heat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word “steak” derives from the Old English “steik,” meaning a stick or spear, as early cuts were often impaled on rods.
The most popular doneness level is medium‑rare, where the internal temperature reaches about 55 °C.
In Japan, “sashimi‑steak” is served raw, sliced paper‑thin, and seasoned with soy and citrus.
Steak quality is often judged by marbling – the intramuscular fat that creates a buttery mouthfeel.
The world’s most expensive steak is Japanese Wagyu, which can reach a BMS (Beef Marbling Standard) of 12.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Steak provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Beef contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Steak supplies B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Zinc and selenium
items.content: These trace minerals aid immune function and protect against oxidative stress.

items.title: Creatine
items.content: Natural creatine in beef helps improve muscular energy production.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Excessive intake may raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: Food‑borne infection risk
items.content: Undercooked steak can harbor pathogens such as E. coli or salmonella.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beef.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: High purine levels can exacerbate gout symptoms.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Steak is typically grilled, pan‑seared, or oven‑roasted to the desired doneness. Let it rest for 5‑10 minutes after cooking so juices redistribute. Serve with sauces, vegetables, potatoes, or fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh steak in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag at –18 °C, where it remains good for 6‑12 months. Thaw in the fridge before cooking.
